title: Query-Specific Causal Graph Pruning Under Tiered Knowledge
one_liner: When you care about one specific causal relationship, you can throw away the irrelevant edges from the full causal graph and identify the effect from less data.
lead: Causal graphs are maps that show which things cause which other things. A real-world graph can have hundreds of connections, but when you ask a specific question (Does this medicine cause that symptom?), most of those edges are clutter. This paper shows how to legally delete irrelevant edges using tiered knowledge — the idea that some causes influence the world in layers — and still get the right answer from data alone.

problem.h2: Full graphs are too big to work with
paras: In the real world, everything affects everything else: your genes affect your health, your diet affects your genes, your exercise affects your diet, pollutants affect all three, and on and on. If you try to map every cause-and-effect, you end up with a tangled mess of hundreds or thousands of arrows.

A beginner would think: just draw every edge, then throw away the ones that do not matter. But here is the trap — you cannot tell which edges matter from data alone. If you see that people who exercise more are healthier, that might be because exercise helps, or because healthier people exercise more, or because both are caused by a third thing like wealth. You cannot distinguish these stories without external knowledge. So most methods force you to specify the entire graph upfront, correctly and completely, before you start.

callout.html: Real causal graphs are enormous, and you must guess the entire structure before you can answer even one question.

steps.text: Does this particular treatment cause this outcome?

paras: The paper changes which edges you need to keep. Instead of keeping the entire causal graph, you keep only the edges that could possibly affect your specific query. All other edges are deleted. This works because some edges are guaranteed to be irrelevant once you specify the tiers and the question.

hidden.h2: Identifiability: when the data alone can answer your question
hidden.name: Identifiability from observational data
paras: Identifiability is the ability to pinpoint a causal effect using only data from observing the world — not from experiments. When you have a causal graph full of confounders (hidden common causes), it is often impossible to identify any single effect, no matter how much data you collect. Your query might be doomed by lurking variables you cannot measure.

This paper measures whether the reduced graph lets you identify the causal effect you care about. If tiered knowledge lets you drop enough edges, the remaining graph becomes simpler — fewer confounders block your query — and suddenly identifiability becomes possible. The paper proves which edges can be safely dropped without breaking identifiability.

heat.caption: Darker edges are closer to your query. Irrelevant edges (light) can be pruned without losing identifiability.

reads.html: Can you figure out the true causal effect from the data you have, or does a confounding variable make it impossible?
The paper proves that edges outside the query-relevant subgraph can be removed while preserving causal identifiability under graphical criteria.

mechanism.h2: Why tiered knowledge lets you prune safely
paras: Confounders — hidden common causes — are what ruin causal discovery. If A and B are both caused by an unmeasured C, then data alone cannot tell whether A causes B or B causes A or neither; the correlation is explained by C. The full causal graph lists every confounder explicitly.

When you organize causes into tiers, you are saying: the confounders within tier 1 can influence everyone, but tier 2 only depends on tier 1 (not on tier 3 or beyond). This structure means that if your query is about the effect of X in tier 2 on Y in tier 3, then edges entirely within tier 1 cannot be on the path from X to Y. You can delete them. Similarly, if your question does not involve Z at all, all edges connected to Z can go. Tiered knowledge gives you permission to delete edges because the structure promises those edges were never on the causal path for your specific question. Fewer edges in the graph means fewer confounders to worry about, which makes identifiability easier — you can prove the effect is real using only the data you have.

stages.s: Full graph, tiers, and your causal query
Find all paths from query source to query target
Mark all edges on these paths as essential
Use tier structure to identify other irrelevant edges
Delete irrelevant edges, keep query-relevant graph
Smaller graph that identifies your specific effect

math.words: A causal effect can be identified if no unobserved confounder blocks all paths from treatment to outcome in the reduced graph.
math.equation: G_reduced = (V, E_essential ∪ E_tier) where E_essential are edges on query paths and E_tier are inter-tier edges needed by structure
symbols: the pruned graph, smaller than the original
edges that lie on at least one path from query source to target
edges between tiers that the causal structure requires
the treatment or cause variable you care about
the outcome variable you want to predict

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Setup: Full graph has 12 variables and 20 edges. Query: Does medicine cause recovery?
Medicine is in Tier 2, recovery is in Tier 3. Paths from medicine to recovery go through 4 intermediate variables.
Essential edges: 8 edges (the medicine -> recovery paths).
Tier edges: 6 edges connect Tier 1 to Tier 2 and Tier 2 to Tier 3.
Irrelevant edges: 20 - 8 - 6 = 6 edges deleted. Reduced graph: 14 edges instead of 20.
Result: Fewer confounders, identifiability becomes possible with less data.

math.note: By deleting edges guaranteed irrelevant by tier structure, the reduced graph has fewer confounders blocking your query path, making causal identification simpler.

charts.title: Naive method (full graph)
charts.note: Full graph forces you to account for every edge. You need many samples to distinguish confounding from real causation.

charts.title: This paper (pruned graph)
charts.note: Tiered pruning removes irrelevant edges upfront. Fewer confounders mean causal identification works with much less data.

items.html: If the tiers do not actually reflect the real causal structure (e.g., tier 2 is secretly influenced by tier 3), then deleted edges might be essential. You will get the wrong answer without knowing it.
If a confounder exists that you never listed in any tier, it can still block your query paths. Pruning edges does not solve this; you still cannot identify the effect.
If you ask the wrong question or define the source and target nodes incorrectly, the pruning will keep the wrong edges and delete the right ones. Garbage in, garbage out.
When tiered knowledge is accurate and you ask a well-defined query, the reduced graph is both smaller and sufficient to identify the causal effect from observational data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulation with a causal graph organized in tiers: tier 1 (unmeasured confounders and background factors), tier 2 (treatment and covariates), tier 3 (outcome). Sample data from this graph. Run the paper's pruning method with a query (e.g., does treatment cause outcome?). Measure: (1) how many edges get deleted, (2) whether the reduced graph still lets you identify the true causal effect, (3) how many samples you need compared to a method that uses the full graph.
demo.metric_eq: Pruning ratio = (edges deleted) / (total edges); Identifiability = true positive rate on causal effects; Sample complexity = min samples for 95% correct identification
demo.closing: The demo should make it clear that removing irrelevant edges does not break your ability to find the true causal effect — it actually makes it easier by giving you fewer confounders to worry about.
